title: doc: Mention partial checksums in Checksum Section

notes.body: mentioned in issue #18864

Fix typo and mention TCP:
```suggestion:-0+0
(__TCP Segmentation Offload (TSO)__ and __Generic Segmentation Offload (GSO)__).
```

Can we also include a link to https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/segmentation-offloads.html somewhere?

Can the text also emphasize that partial checksums are only expected to be seen in packets that are created/transmitted by the capture point? For example:

> Partial checksums are solely seen in packets that were locally generated by the capture point.

> Can the text also emphasize that partial checksums are only expected to be seen in packets that are created/transmitted by the capture point?

I'll emphasize that more. Though isn't that true of all offloaded checksums, so perhaps it should be mentioned more generally in the initial offloading section?

I'm not totally sure how GRO affects captured packets, if it all. It's possible that the kernel socket hands them over for capture as transmitted on the wire. I think I've only seen large packets in the GSO direction.

changed this line in [version 2 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/13275/diffs?diff_id=845465850&start_sha=5e77cf09610f463c7477094a256720e9fc17fbb7#1f045f74268161e75f0284e0e036a6d94fa8c795_1311_1314)

A quick look in the Linux source code shows that Large Receive Offload (LRO) and HW GRO (Hardware Generic Receive Offload) are implemented by the NIC, so in that case the driver/network stack would presumably see one big packet. Not sure about the filled in checksum in that case.

I asked some internal experts, will get back here when I have more details.

BTW, do you think it would be helpful to link to the Linux docs (https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/segmentation-offloads.html)?
I do happen to have some captures lying around captured with GRO active. These packets have a non-zero TCP checksum, which does not match the packet, so is flagged as Bad.

I was told that packets coming from the physical NIC with GRO enabled has a large packet with a checksum covering only the initial packet that is part of the bigger packet. I did not get a packet capture yet, can you test this theory on your capture samples by estimating the original packet size based on MTU?

For packets that originated from the the same machine, the checksum will likely only cover pseudo-headers. That is currently correctly handled as "partial checksum".

Even better, used my ProfiShark to look at the packets on the wire as they came in, while also looking at the packets after GRO collected them. Unfortunately I couldn't find a correlation between the checksum in the packets on the wire and the one found in the amalgamated packet. Not sure what to make of this.
@JaapKeuter are you able to share a pcap with both packet captures?

@@ -1272,14 +1272,17 @@ calculation, also known as checksum offloading. The network driver won’t
 calculate the checksum itself but will simply hand over an empty (zero or
 garbage filled) checksum field to the hardware.
 
-
 [NOTE]
 ====
-Checksum offloading often causes confusion as the network packets to be
-transmitted are handed over to Wireshark before the checksums are actually
-calculated. Wireshark gets these “empty” checksums and displays them as
-invalid, even though the packets will contain valid checksums when they leave
-the network hardware later.
+Checksum offloading often causes confusion as network packets to be
+transmitted are given to Wireshark before they are handed over to the
+hardware. Wireshark gets these “empty” checksums and displays them as
+invalid, even though the packets will contain valid checksums when they
+transit the network.
+
+This only applies to packets that are locally generated by the capture
+point. Received packets will have traveled through network hardware
+and should have correct checksums.
 ====
 
 
@@ -1295,4 +1298,32 @@ You can do two things to avoid this checksum offloading problem:
   Recent releases of Wireshark disable checksum validation by default due to the
   prevalence of offloading in modern hardware and operating systems.
 
+==== Partial Checksums
+
+TCP and UDP checksums are calculated over both the payload and from selected
+elements from the IPv4 or IPv6 header, known as the pseudo header. Linux
+and Windows, when offloading checksums, will calculate the contribution from
+the pseudo header and place it in the checksum field. The driver then directs
+the hardware to calculate the checksum over the payload area, which will
+produce the correct result including the pseudo header's portion of the sum
+as a matter of mathematics.
+
+This precomputation speeds up the hardware checksum calculation later,
+allows the driver to direct the hardware to do checksums over encapsulated
+payloads (__Local Checksum Offload__), and allows applications to send
+the kernel large "superpacket" buffers that will be later divided by
+the hardware into multiple maximum size packets when sent on the network
+(__TCP Segmentation Offload (TSO)__ and __Generic Segmentation Offload (GSO)__).
+
+[NOTE]
+====
+Wireshark 4.2.0 and later can calculate the partial checksum contribution
+from the pseudo header, and when validating TCP and UDP checksums will
+mark partial checksums as valid but partial. The packets with partial
+checksums will not be colored as Bad Checksums by the default coloring rules,
+and will still be used for reassembly. This eliminates spurious checksum
+errors seen on packets transmitted from the capturing host on those platforms
+that use partial checksums when offloading.
+====
+
 // End of WSUG Chapter Advanced
